title: The bread you keep
hookLine: Basil preached that bread you hoard belongs to the hungry

cards: "I will pull down my barns, and will build greater." That's a rich man talking to himself in one of Jesus's parables in Luke. His land has brought in a huge harvest, more than his storage can hold.
So he makes a plan: bigger barns, then rest, eat, drink, be merry. That same night, God tells him his life will be required of him, and asks whose all that grain will be now.
Basil preached a whole sermon on that one sentence, and he started by counting the rich man's pronouns.

teach.h: MY FRUITS, MY BARNS, MY GOODS.
teach.b: First, Basil listens to the rich man's words. My fruits. My barns.
My goods. My soul. He talks only to himself.
He doesn't ask anyone. He doesn't look up from the pile. And Basil asks the question underneath: what is actually yours?
You came into the world with nothing, and you'll leave with nothing. Second, a picture from his city.
Imagine, Basil says, someone who gets to the theater early, takes a seat, and then tries to keep everyone else out, as if a show meant for everyone belonged to him because he arrived first.
That, he says, is what the rich do with what was given for all: they grab it first and then call it theirs. Third, the line that gives today its name. Basil says it plainly to his congregation.

teach.h: THE BREAD BELONGS TO THE HUNGRY.
teach.b: The bread you are keeping belongs to the hungry. The coat you have stored away belongs to the one who has none. The shoes going to waste in your house belong to the barefoot.

The money you have buried belongs to the one in need. He's not saying a barn is evil, or that having things is a sin. He's saying the extra, the part sitting idle while someone goes without, already has an owner.
Fourth, why Catholics still read him.
Catholic teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: the things of the earth are meant for everyone, and owning something carries a duty toward the people who need it.
Basil's sermon said something close to it long before. Read that way, a barn can be a freezer, a pantry, a closet.

how: Catholic parishes often keep food collection boxes and run pantries, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: owning something carries a duty to people in need.

games.q: what does “the bread you keep” mean?
o: Basil's warning that your spare food belongs to the hungry
a parable of Jesus about a widow and her last loaf
the bread a monk sets aside to eat on fast days

games.q: the bread you keep — tap the pairs.
p: I will pull down my barns
grabbing what was meant for all
belongs to the one who has none

s: Basil preached that owning a barn is a sin
he aimed at the extra held back while others go without, not at having things.
Basil compared hoarders to someone keeping others out of theater seats
as if what was meant for all belonged to whoever got there first.
in Luke's parable, the rich man asks others what to do with his harvest
he talks only to himself: my fruits, my barns, my goods.

games.q: you're the rich man in Luke. the harvest is huge and your barns are too small. what does the parable say you do?
o: pull down the barns and build bigger ones.
give the extra to the poor.
sell it and leave the land.
games.why: he builds bigger barns and plans to rest, eat, drink and be merry. that night his life is required of him.

practice: Name, silently, what's in your kitchen the way the rich man would: my cans at the back, my rice nobody has opened, my fruit going soft, and notice how the word my sits.
Then choose one thing that is, in Basil's words, bread you are keeping, and picture where it could go: a pantry box, a neighbor. If you pray, offer it to God before you offer it to them.

wordCard.voice: The bread you keep. Basil's warning that the extra you hold back already belongs to the hungry. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: bread — the bread Basil says belongs to the hungry.

carryVoice: Your line: the hungry own it. What sits idle already has an owner. Back tomorrow.
